transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Well, honestly, what brings me in is... I just cannot keep my mind on one thing anymore. It's getting so bad, and it's really starting to scare me. I've been a carpenter for a long time, and you need to be able to focus when you're doing this kind of work, especially with the machinery and the measurements, but lately, I'll be right in the middle of figuring out a cut list or working on a piece, and just... one saw starting up across the shop will completely derail me. Like, if one of the guys fires up the table saw or even just a little miter saw, my brain is just completely gone from what I was doing. 

Or somebody will just walk past the office window—not even coming in to talk to me, just walking by on their way to the loading dock—and I'll look up and completely lose my train of thought. I'll just sit there wondering what they're doing. And it's not even just stuff happening around me in the shop, it's my own head, too. I'll be working on one cabinet project, and a random thought about another job we have coming up next week will just pop into my head, and suddenly I'm digging through files looking for the blueprints for *that* job, and I've completely abandoned the piece I was actually supposed to be building. It just pulls me entirely off what I’m doing, every single time. And then, before I know it, the whole day just gets away from me. I'll look at the clock and it's 4 PM, and I'll realize I haven't actually finished a single thing I set out to do at 8 AM because I just keep getting pulled away by every little noise or random thought. It's just exhausting trying to get anything done.
Have you struggled with this kind of distractibility and difficulty staying on task your whole life, or is this something that has only started happening more recently?

You know, it is funny you ask that, because I was just thinking about this the other day when I was trying to find a misplaced tape measure. It is definitely not a new thing. Not at all. I mean, my whole life, really. Even way back when I was just a little girl in grade school, definitely before I was even twelve years old, it was the exact same story. 

I remember my mother coming home from parent-teacher conferences, and she would sit me down at the kitchen table—we had this old yellow Formica table—and she would just sigh. Because every single year, the teachers were always telling her the exact same thing. They were always telling my mother that I was bright but careless. Careless, that was the word they always used! And it wasn't that I didn't care, I just... I could not hold onto the things I needed to. I was constantly losing my homework. I would do it, I swear I would do it at home, and then it would just vanish into thin air between my house and the classroom, or it would be crumpled up at the very bottom of my backpack under a bunch of old wrappers. 

Or the teacher would give us instructions for an assignment, you know, do step one, then step two, and by the time she finished talking, I had completely forgotten the instructions. I would just sit there at my desk when I was supposed to be finishing my seatwork, and instead, I would just be staring out the window. I would watch the birds, or the cars going by, or just the clouds, completely lost in my own world while everyone else in the room was actually working. 

So, yeah, it has always been there, just pulling me away from what I am supposed to be doing. It is just that now, with the carpentry and the power tools, the stakes feel so much higher than a lost spelling worksheet, you know? But the feeling itself, that feeling of my brain just floating away and completely losing the thread of what I'm doing... that is exactly the same as when I was eight years old staring out that classroom window.
